All these features appear exclusive to the Pixel 11, though there’s no confirmation from Google on this yet. With the launch of the Pixel 10 series last year, Google introduced long-overdue improvements to Android’s screensaver. The new Screen saver functionality was one of the Pixel 10’s standout features, allowing the idle screen to be turned into a bedside clock or a digital photo frame. And it’s gaining new abilities with the Pixel 11 series. We’ve discovered a new Screen saver style with the Pixel 11 series. title: We tested the Pixel 11’s Tensor G6 chip, and the results are brutal
summary: The G6 is better, but not in the ways it needs to be.
body: I’ll be frank, my hopes for the Tensor G6 were mixed coming into the launch of the Pixel 11 series . Google has made meaningful upgrades to the CPU and TPU for traditional app and AI workloads, respectively, while switching to what should be a more efficient modem. But pairing the Pixel 11 Pro with just 12GB of RAM , down from 16GB last year, undermines its high-end AI credentials. Meanwhile, Google has dropped a CPU core from its configuration, reducing the benefits of its more modern architecture. While we can’t blame Google for the current state of the global RAM supply chain, its decision to switch to yet another mid-range graphics chip is harder to defend. Still, now that we have the phone in hand (and managed to get around Google blocking benchmarks via the Play Store), we’ve been able to run our usual suite of benchmarks to get a feel for where the Pixel 11 series falls in the performance pecking order.

Now, the company is trying to make the passenger experience even better with a useful new feature: Gemini integration. The company has announced that it’s finally bringing Gemini to its cars. Passengers can now use Gemini to control things like the music or cabin temperature. They can also ask Gemini for suggestions about the neighborhood they are driving through or get additional information on a monument or building along their route. body: Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority TL;DR A developer has released an unofficial Android port of Skate 3. The Xbox 360 game runs smoothly on a mid-tier Retroid handheld, and the developer says it’s playable on the sub-$160 ANBERNIC RG406V. The port is quite buggy at the moment, but the developer has already released a few updates. We’ve seen a raft of Xbox 360 games unofficially ported to PC in recent months, and Skate 3 is one of these titles. The popular skateboarding game received two fan ports a few months back, but what about Android? We now have good news on this front. Developer Buku313 released an unofficial Android port of Skate 3 on GitHub this week, dubbed Skate 3 Mobile . This is a fork of the recent Skate3Recomp project for PC. Unlike many other Xbox 360 ports, which often still emulate the GPU, both of these Skate 3 ports have a native Vulkan renderer. In plain English, you can expect fast performance compared to typical fan ports of many Xbox 360 titles.

title: Google begins rolling out Android’s controversial new sideloading flow
summary: The first version of Android’s advanced flow is gradually arriving, with a restart and 24-hour delay built in.
body: TL;DR Google has started rolling out Android’s advanced flow for installing apps from unverified developers. The sideloading process includes a restart and a 24-hour wait, while ADB remains exempt from the verification requirement. The rollout comes ahead of developer verification enforcement, which starts September 30 in four countries. Google’s controversial new rules for installing apps from unverified developers are getting very real fast. We first learned in March that Android would introduce a new process for users who still want to sideload those apps, complete with a 24-hour waiting period. Google has now started rolling out that “advanced flow” ahead of the first checkpoint for developer verification. The news comes from Google’s Android Community Engagement Manager Mishaal Rahman (formerly of this parish), who announced the rollout in a post on the r/Android subreddit . The revamped experience is still in testing, with preview access on Apple TV and Roku and beta access on Android TV; Fire TV support is coming later. Trying to fix what isn’t broken is always a risky choice. There’s always going to be a split among users, with one side critiquing the unnecessary change, and the other side complaining about it never innovating.
